summary: Redwood AE/SE demo covering long-context handling, high TPS concurrency behavior, streaming backpressure and graceful timeout/fallback strategies. Demonstrated Console Optimize suggestions and discussed dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs, KV/prefix caching, and recommended test plan for a pilot.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-05-14 15:00 PT | Duration ~57m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Oliver (Redwood SE), Sofia (Redwood Solutions), Liam (CTO BrightDesk), Priya (ML Eng), Noah (DevOps), Ava (PM)

0:00 Maya: ok folks thanks for joining, we wanted to run through how Redwood behaves when you hit long contexts and heavy concurrency, and how streaming client timeouts are handled, also we'll show some Optimize tips.
0:22 Liam: Sounds good, main thing for us is we have mixed workloads — a long-document summarizer up to 120k tokens and a low-latency chat path, both peak occasionally to ~600 rps across many users.
0:40 Oliver: got it. quick note — when you say 120k you mean upstream chunked inputs? are you pre-chopping or sending as single conversation history? (mumble)
0:55 Priya: most are concatenated history with embeddings + system prompt, we rely on the client to stream in chunks for the long run.
1:12 Maya: perfect. agenda: 1) demo live console run for a long-context session, 2) synthetic TPS ramp to show backpressure, 3) show fallback/timeout behavior and recommended configs.

3:05 Oliver: jumping into the Console — here's the workload profile we uploaded, note the sequence length distribution. we set model variant to redwood-large-quant and enabled KV caching. sometimes the transcript or word is mis-typed as KH cache in earlier notes — that's just transcription.

5:20 Oliver: starting a live generation, you'll see streaming chunks via SSE to the client. by default the streaming window is 250ms flush and 4k chunk aggregation, we can tweak that.

6:10 Priya: quick question — what happens when the client closes the socket after 10s? we saw partial outputs previously and the server charges full token compute?
6:28 Oliver: good question. behavior is: tokens processed up to the last emitted flush are billed and cached. if the connection drops mid-token we try a graceful checkpoint of KV cache; if client reconnects with same session id we can resume from last successful flush. there are subtle cases where partial compute occurs, we add a small safety timeout to rollback some in-flight compute.

9:00 Noah: and timeouts on our side are commonly 15s — will the SDK handle backpressure or do we need retry middleware?
9:18 Maya: SDK has backoff/retry defaults but for streaming we recommend setting a larger read timeout (30s) and enabling automatic reconnection with session ids for resumption; for high TPS we lean on batching + prefix cache to avoid recomputing full context.

12:45 Oliver: switching to the synthetic load test — now ramping from 50 to 600 concurrent requests over 10 minutes targeting a 1.5s token generation per step. you'll see at around 300 concurrent we trigger autoscale burst if Dedicated, or for Hosted we route to best-effort variants.

15:05 (audio distortion) Speaker 1: so is there circuit breaker when latency spikes?
15:17 Oliver: yes, we have request-level queues and per-model concurrency limits; when the queue is full we apply graceful degradation: 1) fall back to a smaller model variant (via routing policy), 2) return a partial answer with a 'truncated' flag, or 3) reject with 503 depending on your chosen fallback policy.

18:40 Liam: do fallbacks keep the same prompt fidelity? i.e., we care about hallucination risk if model size changes mid-session.
18:56 Oliver: good point. fallbacks are configured to use compatible model families where possible and we attach a confidence metadata blob — but yes, model switch can change output distribution. we suggest canarying on a subset of traffic and alerting on quality regression via Optimize evaluations.

22:10 Maya: demonstration — we simulate a long-context session that keeps appending tokens (approx 80k) while we also send 200 parallel short chats. watch the stream behavior and the console trace.

24:02 (typing) Priya: i see a lot of repeated kv hits? what's the cache key strategy?
24:18 Oliver: prefix/KV cache key is based on session id + prompt fingerprint; if you have identical prefix across calls it's a cache hit and cost drops dramatically. note that very long prefixes get chunked for storage efficiency — we keep metadata to rehydrate the KV cache quickly.

27:30 Maya: now intentionally throttle the connection to trigger backpressure — you should see fluid buffering, delayed flushes, and eventual fallback when queue > 1200ms.

29:05 Noah: noticing some partial sentences — is that from the flush window?
29:22 Oliver: yes those are flush boundaries; you can reduce partial sentences by decreasing flush interval or increasing chunk size, but that trades off latency.

32:00 Ava: on the Optimize tab, what suggestions are you surfacing for our profile?
32:12 Oliver: Optimize recommended three things: 1) enable prefix caching for template prompts, 2) lower decoding temperature for short chats and use cached responses for static prompts, 3) for long docs use quantized model variant and increase minibatch for prefix rehydration. you'll see predicted cost savings percent in the UI.

35:40 Priya: about autoscaling — do we get warm pools to avoid cold starts under bursty traffic?
35:55 Oliver: Dedicated supports reserved warm pools and pre-warmed instances; hosted tries to warm based on historical patterns but you can set proactive capacity via reserved contracts. we also support burst capacity for spikes up to N% of committed throughput.

38:50 Liam: ok, what's the recommended test plan to prove latency SLO 95th < 200ms for chat while supporting occasional long-context jobs?
39:07 Maya: test plan: 1) run bench with representative prompt mix (we'll help create), 2) run canary traffic 10% on dedicated, 3) log quality metrics with Optimize evals to detect regressions, 4) tune prefix cache TTL and batch sizing. we'll assemble a concrete schedule.

41:30 (brief crosstalk) Speaker 2: (inaudible) 2nd question, what about SMAL/SSO — SAML integration?
41:48 Maya: we support SAML SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and KMS integrations for Private deployments; our audit logs cover token-level events. implementation details in the security pack we'll share.

44:15 Priya: one last thing — in earlier tests we saw the server return 504 during heavy streaming, is there a swap for retry behavior?
44:30 Oliver: 504s are typically client-side gateway timeouts or proxy cutoffs; we recommend increasing proxy read timeouts for long streaming and using session resumption. on our side we have retry-after headers and optional queueing. if 504 arises from overload we either apply model fallback or a soft-throttle.

48:00 Maya: quick recap and live actions: we'll send dedicated pricing, benchmark template, and schedule the bench run. anything else?
48:15 Liam: please include a sample nginx/proxy config showing timeouts and recommended retry headers.
48:28 Maya: noted.

56:00 Maya: thanks everyone for joining, we'll follow up with links: redwood docs (https://redwood.ai/docs/streaming), bench template (internal link), and security pack (https://redwood.ai/security-pack).
56:22 Meeting end.
